_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a short illustration. 'nonstandard': forms hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.label: Present simple
entries.usage: Habits and general truths.
entries.example: I work here.

entries.label: Present continuous
entries.usage: Happening right now.
entries.example: I am working now.

entries.label: Past simple
entries.usage: A finished past action.
entries.example: I worked yesterday.

entries.label: Future
entries.usage: will / going to.
entries.example: I will come tomorrow.

entries.label: Present perfect
entries.usage: have + past participle.
entries.example: I have finished.

entries.label: Third-person -s
entries.usage: he/she/it adds -s.
entries.example: She works hard.

entries.label: Conditionals
entries.usage: if-clauses.
entries.example: If it rains, I'll stay.

entries.label: Irregular past
entries.usage: Irregular past forms.
entries.example: I went home.

entries.label: To be
entries.usage: For saying what or how somebody is — I am, he is, they are — a word English never drops.
entries.example: I am a student. — Talking about yourself.

entries.label: Commands
entries.usage: For telling or asking somebody to do something, using the plain verb with nobody named in front of it.
entries.example: Open the door, please. — Asking someone to open the door.

entries.label: Do / don't
entries.usage: For turning a statement into a question or a negative by putting do, does or don't in front of it.
entries.example: Do you speak English? — Asking about someone's languages.

entries.label: There is / are
entries.usage: For saying that something exists or is somewhere — one thing takes is, several take are.
entries.example: There is a book on the table. — One thing exists.

entries.label: Continuous vs simple
entries.usage: For choosing between what is going on at this moment and what happens as a rule.
entries.example: The baby is sleeping now, but he usually wakes at six. — Happening this minute, against the usual pattern.

entries.label: Can / have to
entries.usage: For saying what somebody is able to do, what they are allowed to do, and what they have no choice about.
entries.example: She can speak three languages. — Ability now.

entries.label: Passive
entries.usage: For putting the thing something was done to first, when who did it is unknown or beside the point.
entries.example: This wine is produced in Chile. — Present passive.

entries.point: Used to — past habits and states
entries.label: Used to
entries.usage: For something that happened again and again, or was true, in the past but is not any more.
entries.example: I used to play football every weekend. — A past habit, now finished.

entries.label: Reported speech
entries.usage: For passing on what somebody said without quoting their exact words.
entries.example: She said she was busy that evening. — Passing on what she told me.

entries.label: -ing or to
entries.usage: For deciding whether the verb that follows enjoy, want, decide and the rest takes -ing or to.
entries.example: I really enjoy swimming in the sea. — enjoy + -ing.

entries.label: Past conditionals
entries.usage: For imagining how the past could have gone differently, and what would be true now if it had.
entries.example: If you had told me, I would have helped. — Unreal past condition.

entries.label: Must & might
entries.usage: For saying how sure you are about something from the evidence in front of you.
entries.example: The lights are on — someone must be home. — Almost certainly true.

entries.point: Advanced passives (has been done, being done)
entries.label: Advanced passives
entries.usage: For something that was done earlier and still counts now, or is in the middle of being done, when who did it does not matter.
entries.example: The road has been closed since Monday. — Perfect passive.

entries.label: Wishes & regrets
entries.usage: For saying you are sorry something is the way it is now, or was the way it was then.
entries.example: I wish I knew how to drive. — Present regret → past form.

entries.label: Phrasal verbs
entries.usage: For knowing whether the little word can move away from its verb, and where a short word like it has to go.
entries.example: Could you turn it off? The music's too loud. — Pronouns split separable verbs.

entries.label: Question tags
entries.usage: For checking something you already believe (…, aren't you?) and for asking a question the polite, roundabout way.
entries.example: You've met before, haven't you? — Positive → negative tag.

entries.label: Inversion
entries.usage: For dramatic emphasis in formal writing, where a sentence opens with never or not only and the next two words swap round.
entries.example: Never have I heard such nonsense. — Auxiliary before subject.

entries.point: Hedging and distancing (would seem, tend to)
entries.label: Hedging
entries.usage: For making a claim sound careful rather than absolute, the way academic and professional writing expects.
entries.example: It would seem that the figures are wrong. — The classic hedge.

entries.label: Participle clauses
entries.usage: For packing two things the same person did into one sentence: Having finished the report, she left.
entries.example: Having finished dinner, we went for a walk. — The earlier action.

entries.point: The mandative subjunctive (insist that he be)
entries.label: Subjunctive
entries.usage: In formal English, the plain verb stays unchanged for everybody after demand, insist, recommend or suggest.
entries.example: The board insisted that he be removed from the project. — Bare form of be, all persons.

entries.point: Ellipsis and substitution (so, neither, do so)
entries.label: So & neither
entries.usage: For agreeing or answering in short — So do I, Neither can I — instead of repeating the whole sentence.
entries.example: She loved the film, and so did I. — Agreeing without repeating the whole sentence.

entries.label: Plurals
entries.usage: Noun plural forms.
entries.example: box → boxes, child → children

entries.label: Comparatives
entries.usage: -er/-est, more/most.
entries.example: big → bigger → biggest

entries.label: Articles a/an
entries.usage: a before a consonant, an before a vowel.
entries.example: a car, an apple

entries.label: Possessives
entries.usage: my/your and the 's ending.
entries.example: my book, Anna's car

entries.label: Subject pronouns
entries.usage: The words for who is doing something — I, you, he, she, it, we, they — and English can never leave them out.
entries.example: I am from Brazil. — Introducing yourself.

entries.label: Object pronouns
entries.usage: The words for the person or thing on the receiving end, used after a verb or after with, for, to: me, him, us, them.
entries.example: Can you help me, please? — Asking for help for yourself.

entries.point: The — pointing at a specific thing
entries.label: Article the
entries.usage: Use the when both of you already know which one is meant, or when there is only one of it.
entries.example: The sun is hot today. — There is only one of it.

entries.label: Question words
entries.usage: The words that open a question — what, where, when, who, why, how — and always come first.
entries.example: Where do you live? — Asking about someone's home.

entries.label: Some / any
entries.usage: For amounts you are not counting exactly: some in statements and offers, any in questions and negatives, much for what you cannot count and many for what you can.
entries.example: There's some milk in the fridge. — Positive sentence.

entries.label: Frequency adverbs
entries.usage: The words for how often something happens — always, usually, sometimes, never — and where they sit in the sentence.
entries.example: I always drink coffee in the morning — every single day. — 100% of the time.

entries.point: Prepositions of time: in, on, at
entries.label: In / on / at
entries.usage: Which small word goes before a time: at for clock times, on for days and dates, in for months and years.
entries.example: The meeting starts at nine o'clock. — Clock time.

entries.label: Relative clauses
entries.usage: For hanging a description onto a person, thing or place — the woman who lives next door — with who, which, that or where.
entries.example: She's the doctor who treated my father. — A person.

entries.point: Cleft sentences (What I need is…, It was… that)
entries.label: Cleft sentences
entries.usage: For re-shaping a sentence so that one part of it gets the spotlight: What I need is a holiday.
entries.example: What I need is a good night's sleep. — The what-cleft opener.

entries.label: Formal connectors
entries.usage: The joining words that legal and academic writing expects: notwithstanding, albeit, hence, whereby.
entries.example: The plan went ahead, notwithstanding the objections. — Formal 'despite'.
